# KatoANN: Enabling Near-Exact Vector Search at the Speed of Lossy Scans with CPU Matrix Engines ### ABSTRACT Distance scans in partition-family approximate nearest- neighbor (ANN) search are typically limited by memory bandwidth. Existing systems therefore improve throughput by reading fewer bytes per candidate, often at the cost of recall. We present KatoANN, a CPU ANN search system that removes this tradeoff by batching distance scans on Intel AMX, a CPU matrix engine. Batching allows multiple queries to reuse each fetched vector code, shifting the scan from memory-bound to compute-bound and enabling near-exact distances at the speed of a lossy scan. KatoANN stores each vector once as a 16-bit SQ16 code split into high- and low-byte planes. Its adaptive rank-then-refine scan first ranks all candidates using only the high byte, then refines a small survivor set using the full-byte code. Both stages use the same representation, avoiding a second copy of the raw vectors. Experiments across diverse high-dimensional workloads show that KatoANN is the fastest partition-family ANN search system in our evaluation throughout the high- recall range. ### 1 INTRODUCTION Modern AI applications, including retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [28, 29] and recommendation systems [9, 33], answer queries by retrieving nearby embedding vectors with hundreds to thousands of dimensions. At scale, they rely on approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search because exact _K_-nearest-neighbor (KNN) search requires an exhaustive scan of the entire dataset. An effective ANN system must therefore provide high throughput while maintaining recall close to 1, such as 0.99, because any neighbor missed by the search is unavailable to the application. Partition-based search [8, 11, 18, 42], one of the two dominant ANN index families alongside graph-based search [17, 38], spends most of its query time scanning the vectors in the selected partitions. This distance scan is typically _memory-bandwidth-bound_, so its throughput is largely determined by the number of bytes read per candidate. Partition- based ANN systems consequently face a tradeoff between throughput and recall through their choice of vector code, the quantized representation used during the scan. High- precision codes preserve recall but increase memory traffic, whereas low-precision codes reduce memory traffic and improve throughput but may impose a recall ceiling. High-recall configurations in systems such as ScaNN [18] and Faiss [11] attempt to balance this tradeoff through a two- pass design. They first scan compact codes using AVX-512 SIMD instructions, then re-rank a survivor set using full- precision vectors. Although re-ranking improves recall, it requires an additional pass over memory and requires storing the raw vectors alongside the compact codes, reducing throughput and increasing memory usage. This leads us to ask: _Can a partition-based ANN search system achieve high throughput and high recall simultaneously without storing a second vector representation?_ We answer this question affirmatively with KatoANN, a new ANN search system that computes near-exact distances at the speed of a lossy scan while storing each vector only once. The core idea is to batch distance scans on Intel AMX [19], an emerging CPU matrix engine, as illustrated in Figure 1. A distance scan is memory-bandwidth-bound only when each fetched vector serves a small number of queries. CABANA [27], a recent AMX-based ANN system, batches the queries that probe the same cluster, turning the per- query fine scan into matrix multiplication on AMX so that each loaded vector block serves many queries at once. Our key observation is that this batched execution does more than accelerate the scan. <tbc>the scan becomes _compute-bound_, and once computation is the bottleneck, a higher-precision code no longer costs throughput, so the scan has no reason to stay lossy. CABANA leaves this headroom unused. It scans the lossy BF16 code that AMX natively supports, which caps the recall it can reach. KatoANN goes further by computing near-exact distances from SQ16 codes, even though AMX does not natively support 16-bit quantized distance computation.

KatoANN realizes this idea with a high-precision SQ16 representation and an adaptive rank-then-refine scan. Each database vector is kept in one resident form, a 16-bit scalar- quantized (SQ16) code, and each SQ16 coordinate separates into a high byte and a low byte. Because AMX supports INT8 matrix multiplication, KatoANN reconstructs the full SQ16 distance with four INT8 matrix multiplications. This distance is near-exact, but applying all four multiplications to every candidate would waste computation.

KatoANN therefore first ranks all candidates using only the high-byte plane, which requires one matrix multiplication, and then computes the full SQ16 distance only for promising survivors. Because ranking and refinement read the same resident code, no second raw-vector copy is needed. The survivor count is calibrated for each recall target, so lower-recall queries can stop after ranking while higher-recall queries refine only as many candidates as needed. After this design accelerates the fine scan over probed partitions, KatoANN applies the same batched near- exact distance computation to the coarse centroid search as well.

For high-dimensional embeddings, KatoANN further reduces the cost of the ranking stage. A distance-preserving rotation concentrates most of the data variance in the leading dimensions. The ranking stage can then read and process only a short prefix of each vector, while the refinement stage still evaluates promising candidates using all dimensions and the full SQ16 precision. A one-time calibration selects the prefix length and survivor count for each index and recall target, ensuring that each query performs only the work needed to meet its target.

We evaluate KatoANN on diverse high-dimensional workloads. The results show that KatoANN is the fastest partition- based CPU ANN search system in our evaluation across the high-recall range and can match or outperform graph- based systems. For example, on 3,072-dimensional embeddings, KatoANN achieves 15,635 QPS at recall@10 \(\ge\) 0.99, outperforming CABANA and ScaNN by 3.14\(\times\) and 8.45\(\times\), respectively. KatoANN also scales well with additional CPU threads and maintains a small memory footprint by storing only one vector code per database vector.

In summary, we make the following contributions:

\(\bullet\) We show that once batched execution drives the distance scan into the compute-bound regime, lossy codes are no longer needed for high throughput, and we formalize when this crossover occurs.<tbc>

\(\bullet\) We design an adaptive rank-then-refine scan that derives both its cheap ranking key and near-exact refinement distance from a single 16-bit SQ16 code, avoiding a second copy of the vectors.<tbc>

\(\bullet\) We implement KatoANN on a commodity Intel AMX server and show that it is the fastest partition-family CPU search system across the high-recall range on datasets from 96 to 3,072 dimensions.

## 2 BACKGROUND AND MOTIVATION

### 2.1 The Trade-off in the IVF Distance Scan

**Graph search walks, while IVF search scans.** Two index families dominate ANN serving. A graph index walks a proximity graph and compares the query against a small set of visited candidates [17, 31, 38]. An inverted-file (IVF) index instead partitions the database into clusters and scans the inverted lists nearest to the query [8, 11, 18]. The walk visits few candidates, but each step follows a data-dependent pointer and touches scattered memory. The scan evaluates more candidates, but it streams them from contiguous lists, so the work is regular and easy to batch. This regularity also suits continuously updated datasets, since a new vector is appended to one inverted list. For these reasons, this paper targets IVF search.

Once an IVF search selects the clusters to probe, its cost is dominated by the distance scan over their vectors. For high-dimensional embeddings, each comparison touches hundreds to thousands of coordinates. Query cost therefore depends not only on how many candidates are scanned, but also on how efficiently each candidate is evaluated.

**A scan is memory-bandwidth-bound.** The distance scan is a streaming computation. Its inner loop reads a vector code from memory and multiplies it against a query, doing only _O_(1) multiply-add operations per byte it reads. Its speed _T_ follows the roofline model,

\(T\approx min(\pi,I\beta),I=\frac{\# mul-add ops}{\# bytes read},\) (1)

where \(\pi\) is the peak arithmetic rate, \(\beta\) is the memory bandwidth, and _I_ is the arithmetic intensity of the scan.

In a conventional single-query scan, each code is loaded once and used for one distance computation, so _I_ remains low. The scan therefore runs at \(I\beta\), well below the compute peak \(\pi\), and its throughput is largely determined by the number of bytes read per candidate.

**Compact codes sacrifice recall.** The natural way to accelerate a bandwidth-bound scan is to read fewer bytes. IVF<tbc>

<tbc>systems commonly scan compressed or low-precision codes instead of raw vectors. For example, ScaNN \[18\] scores candidates using compact asymmetric-hashing codes, while Faiss \[11\] provides IVF variants based on scalar quantization (SQ) and product quantization (PQ). These codes reduce memory traffic but introduce distance error. The error matters most among nearby candidates, where small score differences determine whether a true neighbor enters the result. At high recall, increasing the number of probed clusters may therefore stop helping because quantization error becomes the limiting factor.

**Reranking adds memory and compute costs.** A common solution is to scan compact codes and rerank the survivors using raw vectors or another more accurate representation. This recovers recall but requires storing the accurate representation alongside the compact codes. It also introduces a second distance pass whose cost grows with the survivor set at higher recall targets.

Other approaches preserve accurate distances while terminating comparisons after enough dimensions have been examined \[10, 13\]. Although they avoid arithmetic on many candidates, their candidate-dependent and branch-heavy execution does not map well to dense batched computation.

## 2.2 A Case of AMX-Accelerated ANN

KatoANN is an AMX-accelerated ANN search system. We here explain why AMX with batching is the right approach.

**Batching changes the scan to compute-bound.** One assumption for the bandwidth bound is that each loaded vector code serves a single query. However, modern ANN search in data centers should handle multiple concurrent<tbc>

<tbc>queries that can probe the same inverted lists. Therefore, after cluster-aware grouping \[27\], a block of vector codes can be loaded once and multiplied against an effective group of _M_<sub>eff</sub> queries that probe the same list. The arithmetic intensity then rises from _I_≈1 to _I≈M_<sub>eff</sub>, because the same bytes are reused across many queries. By Eq. 1, the scan becomes _compute-bound_ once

\(M_\mathrm{eff}\unknown M^\star=\frac{\pi}{\beta}.\) (2)

Here _M_<sub>eff</sub> is not the total request batch size, but the number of queries that reuse the same candidate block after cluster- aware grouping. When this reuse is large enough, throughput is determined by how many multiply-add operations the CPU can execute, not by how few bytes each vector code stores. At that point, the scan no longer needs to sacrifice precision just to reduce memory traffic.

Figure 3 measures this transition with a BF16 distance kernel on our AMX server (_d_=1024, 2M vectors, 32 threads); CABANA reports the same shape at low dimension. At a batch of 16 queries, AMX delivers only 1.3\(\times\) the AVX-512 rate; as each loaded code block serves more queries, the gap widens to about 14\(\times\) at a batch of 1,024. The engine alone therefore buys little, and the cross-query reuse is what lifts the scan off the bandwidth roof.

**AMX matches distance scans.** A compute-bound batched scan requires a unit that can execute many multiply-add operations in parallel. The AVX-512 SIMD units that existing IVF systems use for the scan compute multiply-add operations over one-dimensional vector registers. A matrix engine executes far more operations per instruction, because<tbc>

<tbc>it multiplies one two-dimensional block against another. Recent Intel CPUs provide such an engine through Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) [19]. Figure 2 shows the engine and how the batched scan maps onto it. AMX provides two-dimensional _tile_ registers and tile-multiply instructions that multiply a block of queries by a block of vector codes, accumulating a dense result block. This shape matches the IVF distance scan. For each probed cluster, the database vectors form a contiguous candidate block, and the queries that probe the cluster form the other dimension of the matrix multiply.

AMX, however, directly supports only low-precision operands such as INT8 and BF16. This operand restriction creates the central precision problem for AMX-based high- recall ANN search. CABANA [27] demonstrates the performance opportunity by mapping the cluster-aware IVF fine scan to AMX-efficient matrix multiplication, but it still scans a lossy BF16 code because that format is directly supported by AMX. This leaves the precision problem unresolved and harms retrieval quality since recall is limited. KatoANN instead keeps the scan compute-bound on the matrix engine by decomposing each SQ16 code into two INT8 planes and using AMX multiply-add operations to compute near-exact distances, despite AMX’s lack of native SQ16 support.

**Comparison with existing approaches.**  1 summarizes the design space. CABANA is fast and memory- efficient but can limit recall. IVF-Flat preserves accurate distances but incurs high compute and memory costs. ScaNN recovers recall through reranking but stores both compact codes and raw vectors. ADSampling and DADE reduce arithmetic but do not map cleanly to dense AMX execution. KatoANN combines high recall, high throughput, and a small<tbc>

<tbc>memory footprint by deriving both its inexpensive ranking distance and near-exact refinement distance from one resident SQ16 code.

## 3 KATOANN DESIGN

### 3.1 System Overview

KatoANN is a partition-family ANN search system built around one design principle. Each database vector is stored only once, as a resident SQ16 code, and every scan stage derives its distances from that code. This principle eliminates the common split between a compact lossy scan code and a second raw vector copy for refinement. The remaining challenge is to make this higher-precision code fast on a CPU matrix engine that natively favors low-precision operands. KatoANN addresses this challenge by turning the IVF scan into a dense batched matrix computation and by paying the full SQ16 distance only where it is needed.

The design proceeds by removing the cost that would otherwise appear after the previous step.

\(\bullet\) First, AMX can efficiently execute dense low-precision matrix multiplies, but it does not natively support the SQ16 precision required for high recall. KatoANN therefore splits each SQ16 coordinate into two byte planes whose four INT8 partial products recombine into the SQ16 dot product. This makes near-exact SQ16 distance available on a low-precision matrix engine.<tbc>

\(\bullet\) Second, computing this full SQ16 distance for every probed candidate would waste computation, because most candidates are far from the final top-_K_. KatoANN therefore uses a recall-adaptive rank-then-refine cascade. A cheap<tbc>

**Life of a query batch.** Figure 4 shows how a batch moves through KatoANN. A serving batch first enters the coarse search, which scores the batch against all centroids and selects the nprobe nearest clusters per query. KatoANN then inverts the schedule from query order to cluster order. Each cluster is scanned once, in one dense matrix multiply against all the queries that probe it. The fine scan orders the probed candidates by the high-byte key. At lower recall targets this ordering already yields the final top-_K_; at higher ones the top \(S=R\cdot K\) per query continue into the full SQ16 refinement, where _R_ is the survivor factor determined by a one- time calibration. For high-dimensional data, the calibration also chooses the prefix length _d_<sub>0</sub> per recall target.

## 3.2 Byte-Split and Rank-then-Refine

**SQ16 as the scan code.** The matrix engine reaches its highest throughput on low-precision operands such as INT8 and BF16. Using those formats directly is fast, but it can blur the close-distance candidates that decide recall near exact KNN. KatoANN therefore stores each coordinate as a 16-bit scalar- quantized code, SQ16, as Figure 5 (a) illustrates. Unlike BF16, which spends many bits on exponent range, SQ16 uses the full 16-bit grid to resolve values within the data range. The resulting distance is not bit-identical to FP32, but it is near- exact for ANN ranking in our target regime. The problem is that AMX has no native 16-bit integer matrix multiply. The byte split below is what lets KatoANN keep SQ16 precision while still executing on the engine’s INT8 path.

Let an SQ16 coordinate be written as _x_=2<sup>8</sup>_x<sub>h</sub>+x<sub>l</sub>_ and _q_=2<sup>8</sup>_q<sub>h</sub>+q<sub>l</sub>_. Then the dot product decomposes as

\(\langle q,x\rangle=2^{16}\langle q_h,x_h\rangle+2^8\big(\langle q_h,x_l\rangle+\langle q_l,x_h\rangle\big)+\langle q_l,x_l\rangle.\) (3)

Each term is an INT8 matrix multiply over byte planes, and the shifted sum reconstructs the full SQ16 dot product. For _L_<sub>2</sub>, KatoANN combines this dot product with cached per- vector terms and per-batch query terms:

\(\|q-x\|^2=\|q\|^2+\|x\|^2-2\langle q,x\rangle.\) (4)

The affine SQ16 scale and zero point are applied after recombination; terms independent of the query are cached with the vector code.

**Why two byte planes suffice.** The byte split does not approximate the SQ16 code. It is the exact two-byte representation of the code. Thus, four partial products are enough to reconstruct the SQ16 dot product, with no additional rounding after SQ16 quantization. Each INT8 tile multiply accumulates into INT32; KatoANN promotes the partial sums before the 2<sup>8</sup> and 2<sup>16</sup> shifts, avoiding overflow for the dimensions we target. For UINT8-native datasets, KatoANN dispatches directly to the native byte dot product. For cosine distance, KatoANN uses the same path on normalized vectors.

**One code, two precisions.** The full byte split provides the precision needed for high recall while naturally exposing a cheaper ranking key. The high-by-high term \(\langle q_h,x_h\rangle\) is one of the four SQ16 partial products and, together with cached high-byte norms, gives the exact _L_<sub>2</sub> distance between the high-byte truncations of the query and database vector. This key is not computed from a separate lossy representation. It comes from the same SQ16 code and requires reading only the high-byte plane. Thus, KatoANN can first rank candidates using a partial view of the SQ16 code and compute the full SQ16 distance only where necessary.

<tbc>the work on candidates that cannot enter the final top-_K_. Figure 5 (b) shows how KatoANN separates ranking from refinement. Phase 1 ranks all probed candidates using the high-byte key, requiring one INT8 product stream per candidate. If this ranking is sufficient for the target recall, KatoANN directly returns its top-_K_. Otherwise, Phase 2 selects the top _S=R-K_ candidates from the high-byte ranking, computes their full four-term SQ16 distances, and chooses the final top-_K_ from the refined set.

**Calibrating the cascade.** The survivor factor _R_ is calibrated for each index and recall target. Using a labeled query sample, calibration jointly sweeps npprobe and _R_, with the full byte-split scan serving as the precision reference. npprobe determines coverage by controlling which clusters are scanned, whereas _R_ determines how many candidates within those clusters receive the full SQ16 distance. The calibration selects the smallest _R_, including no refinement, that reaches the target recall.

**Why the cascade stays near the cost of a lossy pass.** For _N_ probed candidates, a full byte-split scan performs four INT8 product streams per candidate, for a total cost of 4_N_. The cascade instead performs one stream for all candidates and four streams for only the \(R\cdot K\) survivors, yielding dominant work of _N_ + 4_RK_. Because the INT8 ranking pass also packs more coordinates into each tile than a BF16 pass, its bulk scan is no more expensive than a conventional low-precision scan over the same candidates. The additional SQ16 work is confined to a small survivor set and is incurred only when the target recall requires refinement.

## 3.3 Feeding the Matrix Engine

The SQ16 cascade reduces arithmetic, but it only helps if the matrix engine is kept busy. KatoANN uses two mechanisms for this feed problem. As illustrated in Figure 6, cluster-to- query inversion creates reuse across queries that probe the same list, and the VNNI-order code layout makes each AMX tile load contiguous.

**Cluster-to-query inversion.** AMX multiplies a query tile, the A-tile, by a code tile, the B-tile, and accumulates a block of distances. To use this shape efficiently, the scan needs many queries to share the same code tile. A naive per-query IVF loop does the opposite; it scans the probed lists of each query separately, so codes stream repeatedly with little reuse and the query tile is often underfilled. KatoANN therefore groups work by cluster. For each cluster _c_, it gathers the _M<sub>c</sub>_ queries in the batch that probe _c_ and scans the cluster once against those queries. The expected reuse is

\(M_c\approx\frac{B\cdot\text{nprobe}}{\text{nlist}},\) (5)

up to skew in centroid popularity, where _B_ is the request batch size. When _M<sub>c</sub>_ is large, a loaded code block is reused across many queries, increasing arithmetic intensity and moving the scan toward the compute-bound regime. When _M<sub>c</sub>_ is small, KatoANN still executes the same loop with shorter tiles rather than padding all clusters to a fixed size. The scan is blocked so that the active query tile and code tile stay close to the core while the inverted list is streamed.

**VNNI-order multi-bit code layout.** Cluster-to-query inversion creates the right computation, but the engine can still stall if each B-tile has to be assembled from scattered memory locations. A dimension-major layout is natural for a single-query SIMD loop, because it stores the coordinates of one vector consecutively. For AMX, however, the B-tile consumes a byte stripe across a block of database codes and dimensions. If the codes remain in dimension-major order, the runtime must gather strided pieces to form every tile. KatoANN therefore stores each cluster in a VNNI-order tensor whose innermost block matches the B-tile stripe. The build cost is a permutation pass per cluster. At query time, each tile load reads a contiguous byte stripe, and the same layout serves both the high-byte ranking pass and the full byte-split refinement.

## 3.4 Batched Coarse Search and Selection

**The new bottleneck.** IVF search first chooses the nearest centroids, then scans their inverted lists. When the fine scan is slow, the centroid scan and top-_K_ maintenance are usually hidden behind the scan cost. After the SQ16 cascade and AMX batching reduce the fine-scan cost, these surrounding stages become visible and can cap throughput. KatoANN therefore applies the same design rule to the rest of<tbc>

<tbc>the pipeline, keeping dense distance computation on the matrix engine and scalar selection work off the critical path.

**All-centroid routing as a dense scan.** One way to reduce coarse-search cost is to add a secondary approximate router, but that introduces query-dependent control flow and another source of routing error. KatoANN instead scores every centroid for every query in the batch. This is feasible because the centroid table is small compared with the database, and it has the same dense shape as an inverted list that every query probes. At build time, KatoANN quantizes centroids into SQ16 and stores their high and low byte planes in the same VNNI-order layout as database codes. At query time, the coarse search becomes a dense batched byte-split scan over all centroids, followed by a per-query partial selection of the nearest nprobe centroids. This introduces no additional routing loss from an approximate router, because every centroid is scored under the same SQ16 distance model used by the fine scan. The cost is flat in nprobe, so the same routing path supports both moderate and high recall targets.

**Keeping selection off the critical path.** Once distance computation becomes cheap, a scalar heap can dominate. KatoANN uses two selection paths because the best way to avoid heap overhead depends on the probe regime. At high probe counts, each query sees many candidates, so its current _K_-th-best distance \(\tau_K\) tightens quickly. KatoANN uses threshold-guarded selection, in which a SIMD compare rejects distances larger than \(\tau_K\) before they reach the heap. The compare runs on vector units while AMX continues producing later distance tiles, so most candidates are discarded without stalling the matrix engine.

At low probe counts, the candidate pool is smaller and \(\tau_K\) remains loose. In this regime, threshold rejection is less effective because many distances still pass the guard. KatoANN instead keeps a small insertion-sorted array of the best \(S=R\cdot K\) candidates per cluster and merges those local lists across clusters. This local selection is exact for the global top-_S_, because a query’s global top-_S_ must be contained in the union of the per-cluster top-_S_ sets. The local path replaces data-dependent heap updates with short inregister insertions and switches back to threshold guarding when the probe count is large.

## 3.5 Dimension Cascade

The rank-then-refine cascade reduces precision cost, but on high-dimensional embeddings the ranking pass can still dominate because it touches every probed candidate. Even a one-stream high-byte pass becomes expensive when each candidate has hundreds to thousands of coordinates. KatoANN therefore adds a dimension cascade. It ranks all candidates using only a short prefix, then refines the survivors using the full vector.

A naive prefix would discard useful signal arbitrarily. At build time, KatoANN applies an orthogonal rotation that concentrates variance into leading coordinates while preserving full-dimensional distances before quantization. The ranking pass then uses only the first _d_<sub>0</sub> dimensions of the high-byte plane. This reduces the work paid for every candidate, which is the dominant cost of the ranking stage. The refinement pass still uses all _d_ dimensions of the SQ16 code, so the prefix affects only which candidates reach refinement, not the final distance used for high-recall ranking.

The prefix length _d_<sub>0</sub> and survivor factor _R_ are calibrated together. A smaller prefix reduces ranking cost but may require more survivors because the prefix ordering is less sharp. A larger prefix costs more per candidate but gives a more reliable ordering and can reduce the survivor set. The plain cascade is the special case _d_<sub>0</sub>=_d_, where no dimensions are dropped and the ranking pass uses the full high- byte vector. The calibration selects this case automatically when the data does not compress well, and selects a shorter prefix when the variance concentrates in the leading coordinates. The result is a cascade that becomes cheap in both bits and dimensions for the candidates seen by the ranking pass, while the final refinement remains full-dimensional.

## 3.6 Discussion

**Hardware portability.** The implementation in this paper targets Intel AMX, but the structure is more general. The design requires a low-precision matrix engine, a way to feed it dense tiles, and enough accumulator precision to recombine byte-split partial products safely. Such engines are becoming a standard CPU feature rather than an Intel-only one. Arm ships a comparable unit today through the Scalable Matrix Extension (SME2) of Armv9 CPUs. We therefore expect the byte-split decomposition and the cascade to apply on these engines, subject to their operand types and accumulator widths.

**Scaling beyond a single server.** KatoANN is a per-shard, in-memory ANN search system, but larger data can be partitioned across multiple servers. This distributed setting preserves two key properties of the design. First, KatoANN’s throughput advantage comes from reducing the cost of each distance comparison, so it does not depend on the total collection size. We therefore expect the per-shard advantage to remain as more shards are added. Second, Eq. 2 becomes a placement constraint. A shard remains compute-bound only when enough concurrent queries reuse its resident lists. The distributed front end should therefore route queries in a way that preserves the effective batch size seen by each shard, and cluster placement should keep frequently co-probed clusters on the same shard to maintain list reuse.

## 4 IMPLEMENTATION

KatoANN is implemented in about 9KLoC of C++17 and 2KLoC of x86 intrinsics. A small dispatch layer selects the datatype, metric, and scan mode at runtime. The code builds with GCC 13 and oneAPI 2024, requires no kernel patches, and enables AMX tile state once at startup through the standard ARCH\_REQ\_XCOMP\_PERMarch\_prctl request.

**Kernels.** The AMX scan kernels are written directly with tile intrinsics. The BF16 path uses \_tile\_dpbf16ps. The SQ16 byte-split path uses \_tile\_dpbuud for unsigned INT8 partial products and \_tile\_loadd for VNNI-order tile loads. The full byte-split scan, cascade, batched coarse search, and dimension cascade share the same kernel templates, differing only in the byte planes and dimensions fed to the tile multiply. A one-time calibration selects the scan mode and parameters per built index; serving performs no per-query mode search.

**Runtime.** For each query batch, KatoANN rebuilds the cluster-to-query map in place in \(O(M\cdot\) nprobe) using an indexed bucket array. Worker threads take clusters round- robin and keep heaps and scratch buffers private, so the scan path requires no inter-thread synchronization. Top-_K_ filtering runs on AVX-512 with \_mm512\_cmp\_ps\_mask, skipping empty 32-candidate blocks and pushing only surviving lanes into the heap.

**Storage and build.** Each cluster is stored as a VNNI-order tensor whose innermost stripe matches the AMX B-tile. The same layout is used for database lists and centroids. Index construction is a streaming pass over the input vectors; the builder assigns clusters and emits SQ16 codes, high- byte norms, centroid codes, and packed tensors inline. The packed tensors can be memory-mapped; in the evaluated in-memory regime, the active shard remains resident after warm-up.

## 5 EVALUATION

### 5.1 Methodology

**Testbed.** All experiments run on a 2-socket Intel Xeon Silver 4514Y server (Emerald Rapids, 32 physical cores / 64 logical cores) with 256 GB DDR5 and NVMe storage. The host runs Ubuntu 24.04 with kernel 6.14. Every system runs with _T_=32 pinned threads, the performance governor, memory interleaved across both sockets, and a 10K-query warm-up. We measure KatoANN and each baseline interleaved within one session and report the median of three repetitions, with a per-point coefficient of variation below 2%.

**Datasets.**  2 lists the 8 datasets used in evaluation. DEEP-96 [4] is a typical low-dimensional benchmark dataset.

The other datasets contain 768- to 3072-dimensional embeddings and scale up to 10M vectors. Cohere-768 and OpenAI- 1536-5M come from the VectorDBBench suite [48]; the former embeds 2022-12 English Wikipedia passages with Cohere’s multilingual model, and the latter embeds the C4 corpus with a 1536-dimensional OpenAI model. BioASQ- 1024 is VectorDBBench’s 1024-dimensional embedding of the BioASQ biomedical corpus. Cohere-1024 embeds the 2023-11 Wikipedia dump with Cohere embed-multilingual- v3. OpenAI-1536-1M and OpenAI-3072-1M embed DBpedia entity abstracts with OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 and text-embedding-3-large, respectively. The high-dimensional sets are FP32 under cosine similarity and are served as _L_<sub>2</sub> search on normalized vectors. For every dataset, we compute the exact top-10 neighbors by exhaustive FP32 search under the same metric used for serving. For cosine datasets, both database and query vectors are normalized before ground-truth construction, so the _L_<sub>2</sub> ranking preserves the cosine ranking.

**Compared systems.** We compare against both partition- family and graph-family systems. The partition family comprises CABANA, ScaNN, and Faiss FastScan. CABANA [27] is the prior AMX-based ANN system. We faithfully reimplement its published design, which batches queries onto MKL’s BF16 GEMM through hash-grouped cluster-to-query inversion. We validate the reimplementation by matching the reported grouping-overhead share and by confirming that its speedup over an AVX-512 FP32 baseline lands within the published range on CABANA’s own low- dimensional datasets. ScaNN [18] is the AVX-512 partition baseline, swept over its leaves-and-reorder grid. Faiss [11] runs FastScan with IVF , PQx4fs and FP32 refine.

The graph family spans FP32 Vamana [38] (_R_=128) and HNSW [31] with raw vectors resident, the quantized-code graph SVS [1] (Vamana, degree 64, window 200) with one- and two-level LVQ codes and the reduced-dimension Lean- Vec configuration [39], and the disk-resident DiskANN and PipeANN [17] for completeness. The high-byte-only scan reads one byte plane in one INT8 product stream and is the fastest at matched recall through the moderate band. The dimension cascade is the same cascade with its ranking pass run on a rotated reduced-dimension prefix. On this compressible high-dimensional data it runs above the plain cascade through the high-recall band and raises the served curve to 15,635 QPS at recall 0.99 on OpenAI-3072-1M. KatoANN serves the recall-adaptive envelope of these modes, fixed once per index by calibration. The calibrated served

curve follows the fastest measured mode at each operating point in our sweep.

**The cascade returns the same neighbors as the full scan.** The cascade is a safe speedup only if its survivor set keeps the true neighbors, so we compare it against the full byte-split scan on all eight FP32 sets. Figure 12 reports the largest recall gap over \(K\in\{10,100\}\) and nprobe \(\in\{64,256,512\}\). With the calibrated _R_=2, the cascade reproduces the full scan’s recall on every set, with a maximum gap of 0.01 recall points. Removing the over-fetch margin (_R_=1) loses up to 5.0 points. This is because the margin, not the high-byte ordering alone, covers the rare cases where a true neighbor falls just below the top-_K_ boundary of the ranking. Though omitted, larger factors recover nothing further; _R_=3 and _R_=4 return identical recall at lower throughput, so _R_=2 is a saturation point rather than a sensitive threshold.

## 6 RELATED WORK

**Matrix-engine and accelerated search.** CABANA [27] is the closest system to KatoANN. It batches IVF cluster scans onto Intel AMX with cluster-aware query grouping. However, it scans lossy BF16 codes, so its recall caps below the

high-recall band. KatoANN instead ranks and refines from a single resident SQ16 code, so no recall ceiling appears in our measured range. ScaNN [18] and Faiss FastScan [2, 11] accelerate the partition scan with AVX-512 SIMD units, which compute distances for one query at a time. GPU-based ANN search systems [21, 26, 34] move the scan to a separate, expensive device. KatoANN instead targets the matrix engine already present in the CPU.

**Quantization, refinement, and distance pruning.** Most systems reduce scan cost with compressed codes, including product quantization [20], anisotropic quantization [18], LVQ and LeanVec [1, 39], and bit-level RaBitQ [12, 14]. High- recall operation then usually adds a re-ranking stage against a second, more precise representation. SVS-LVQ is the closest in mechanism, since it also refines from a compact code, but it does so along a graph walk that a matrix engine cannot accelerate. ADSampling [13], DADE [10], and TRIM [37] instead stop distance computations early, a per-candidate control flow that does not map to dense tiles. KatoANN differs by drawing both the cheap ranking key and the full refinement from one SQ16 byte-split code, so it needs no second copy and no early-stopping shortcut.

**Graph, storage, and database systems.** Graph indexes [17, 31, 38] reduce the number of comparisons by walking a proximity graph, which is complementary to KatoANN’s cheaper comparisons. Out-of-core and near-storage systems [8, 25, 40, 41, 44, 46], filtered search [5, 16, 23, 30, 35, 36, 43], adaptive partitioning [32], vector databases [24, 42, 47], and RAG pipelines [3, 6, 7, 15, 22, 45] optimize placement, query semantics, or application pipelines, all orthogonal to per-distance compute. KatoANN can serve as the high- throughput distance engine inside such systems.

## 7 CONCLUSION

We presented KatoANN, an AMX-accelerated ANN search system that simultaneously achieves high throughput, high recall, and a small memory footprint. KatoANN stores each vector only once as an SQ16 code, ranks candidates using a low-cost high-byte key, and adaptively refines only the survivors with the full byte-split SQ16 distance on Intel AMX. Our evaluation shows that KatoANN is the fastest partition- family system among those tested across the high-recall range. More broadly, this work establishes CPU matrix engines as a promising foundation for ANN serving. They support high-throughput, high-recall vector search beyond the AVX-512 SIMD designs that existing systems use.
